title: Ministers on air quality: targets, farming ammonia and transport
label: 14 September 2026 · Air Pollution in England (condensed)
summary: Ministers from the Department for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs (DEFRA) and the Department for Transport (DfT) answered the committee on how government is tackling air pollution. They discussed cross-government working, revising targets for fine particles (PM2.5), monitoring expansion, how to cut farming ammonia (a key source of pollution), the role of non-exhaust road emissions like brake and tyre wear, measures for ports and shipping, and how the Government supports local authorities considering schemes such as low-emission zones.

chapters.title: Intro and cross-government working
chapters.takeaway: Ministers admit cross-department work on air quality needs strengthening and plan a formal group as they produce a 2028 air quality strategy.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Welcome. Could the Ministers introduce themselves and say how well Government departments are working together on air pollution?

turns.speaker: Simon Lightwood
turns.text: I'm Simon Lightwood from DfT, responsible for buses and local transport; I'm joined by Jennifer Raynor.

turns.speaker: Jennifer Raynor
turns.text: I'm Jennifer Raynor from DfT, working on environment and adaptation strategy.

turns.speaker: Emma Hardy
turns.text: I'm Emma Hardy, Minister at DEFRA, and with me is Bill Parish from DEFRA who handles agriculture and industrial pollution.

turns.speaker: Bill Parish
turns.text: Good afternoon.

turns.speaker: Emma Hardy
turns.text: On cross-government working: it's not perfect. We're launching a call for evidence this year ahead of an air strategy due in 2028, and we want a formal cross-Department group to sort trade-offs and coordinate policy.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: So you accept it needs improvement and will pursue stronger co-ordination—good.

chapters.title: Targets, monitoring and Ella’s law
chapters.takeaway: DEFRA wants to refocus targets on the most harmful pollutants and keep pushing improvement after local areas meet minimum legal limits.

turns.speaker: Julia Buckley
turns.text: On Ella's law (which wants everyone protected no matter where they live): how are you bringing its ideas into future law or policy?

turns.speaker: Emma Hardy
turns.text: I support Ella's ambition. Practically, we're rethinking targets and how we measure pollutants so we focus on what's most harmful today, not just older measures. We also want a mindset of continuous improvement instead of 'you met the limit, job done.'

turns.speaker: Julia Buckley
turns.text: So beyond just meeting a minimum standard, will you focus on the unequal exposure in deprived areas?

turns.speaker: Bill Parish
turns.text: Yes. For fine particles (PM2.5 — tiny particles that penetrate lungs) we set a national long-term target of 10 micrograms per cubic metre by 2030, matching EU levels, and a population exposure reduction target (PERT) to cut exposure by 30% from 2018 levels by 2030.

turns.speaker: Julia Buckley
turns.text: Is the 30% an average or will you target deprived hotspots?

turns.speaker: Bill Parish
turns.text: PERT is national, but we're expanding monitoring in population hotspots. Since 2024 we've added 65 PM2.5 monitors and plan about 197 by end of 2027 to get finer local data. We're also piloting vulnerability maps with the UK Health Security Agency to show which deprived communities are worst affected so local action can be focused.

turns.speaker: Julia Buckley
turns.text: Who pays for local action in deprived areas?

turns.speaker: Emma Hardy
turns.text: That mainly comes via local government funding (that's the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government's area), so we work with them but they manage local finance.

chapters.title: Nitrogen and farming ammonia
chapters.takeaway: Ammonia from farming is the biggest nitrogen source; ministers favour support-plus-regulation, expanding permits and grants rather than wholesale buy-outs seen abroad.

turns.speaker: Manuela Perteghella
turns.text: Nitrogen harms nature and health. Will DEFRA publish a national nitrogen strategy that joins air, water, climate and biodiversity?

turns.speaker: Emma Hardy
turns.text: Nitrogen spans many issues. We don't have a single new national strategy planned; instead we use existing plans (environmental improvement plan, farming roadmap, water work) and we’re watching approaches like Scotland's nitrogen balance sheet.

turns.speaker: Manuela Perteghella
turns.text: Are you working with DfT and the energy department to make sure approaches are coherent?

turns.speaker: Emma Hardy
turns.text: Yes — we're coordinating across departments and with farmers, but ammonia is tricky and politically sensitive.

turns.speaker: Bill Parish
turns.text: To be clear: some countries like the Netherlands and Denmark have used stronger actions, including paying farmers to stop, which has been politically hard. Our approach is to work with farmers, use grants and consider extending environmental permitting (a regulatory permission system) to sectors such as beef and dairy to cut ammonia.

turns.speaker: John Whitby
turns.text: How are you supporting farmers to adopt ammonia-cutting practices without wrecking their businesses? Will rules on fertiliser use and storage be mandatory, not just voluntary?

turns.speaker: Emma Hardy
turns.text: We're offering money and support: the Farming Equipment and Technology Fund had £46.7 million, with £30 million for equipment that helps slurry management to cut ammonia; we added another £10 million in 2026. We're consulting on bringing beef and dairy into permitting — that adds rules, but will be paired with grants and support so farms can adapt.

turns.speaker: Barry Gardiner
turns.text: Countries like the Netherlands cut ammonia a lot through housing, covered stores and spreading tech, not just closures. Our reductions are only about 9% in 21 years versus much bigger cuts elsewhere. Are we doing enough and why has the UK sometimes resisted stronger international ammonia rules?

turns.speaker: Emma Hardy
turns.text: We can do more on ammonia. We work with farmers, increase inspections via the Environment Agency, use grants and are preparing permitting proposals. We haven't adopted large-scale buy-outs like the Netherlands.

turns.speaker: Bill Parish
turns.text: I agree the AQ Expert Group shows technical measures work. We're looking to combine grants and a regulatory approach to make faster progress, especially given the cattle sector contributes about 46% of UK ammonia emissions.

chapters.title: Public alerts and communication
chapters.takeaway: A new opt-in air quality alert launched in July; ministers want wider public awareness but currently it relies on sign-ups and partner organisations to spread the word.

turns.speaker: Barry Gardiner
turns.text: You launched a phone alert scheme in August — how many signed up by end of that month?

turns.speaker: Emma Hardy
turns.text: I thought it was around 2,500, but the written answer shows 525 had signed up by that date — it's very new, launched 30 July.

turns.speaker: Barry Gardiner
turns.text: Why is it opt-in only? Heat and flood warnings go out widely via the Met Office. People should be told when air reaches illegal levels, not shown a chart that calls illegal levels 'low'.

turns.speaker: Emma Hardy
turns.text: The new alert is opt-in like flood alerts. We're also using the Air Pollution Awareness Coalition (APAC), which brings health groups and charities together, to improve public messaging. Bill explained that the daily air quality bands warn about short-term spikes, while legal limits are year-long averages — that causes confusion.

turns.speaker: Bill Parish
turns.text: Yes: legal limit values are about long-term averages. The daily air quality index (DAQI) is for short-term spikes and health warnings on bad days; both are important but different things.

chapters.title: Transport, non-exhaust emissions and local measures
chapters.takeaway: DfT backs the Euro 7 approach to regulate brake and tyre particles (non-exhaust) and supports electrification plus better public transport; local authorities decide low-emission zones, with Government funding support.

turns.speaker: Barry Gardiner
turns.text: Non-exhaust sources — brake, tyre and road wear — stay after electrification. How will you bring UN brake emissions rules into UK law and align with Euro 7?

turns.speaker: Simon Lightwood
turns.text: DfT consulted on adopting Euro 7, which for the first time would regulate brake and tyre wear particles. We supported research to back this and will publish our response soon. We propose new brake emission rules for new cars and vans from 29 November 2027.

turns.speaker: Sojan Joseph
turns.text: What about emissions from shipping near ports — are you assessing impacts on coastal communities and doing enough?

turns.speaker: Simon Lightwood
turns.text: We act domestically and internationally. The IMO (the UN body for shipping) sets limits; a new north Atlantic emission control area was adopted and will cover UK waters by 2028, giving the highest control level for shipping emissions.

turns.speaker: Jennifer Raynor
turns.text: We're also asking ports through a “Net Zero Ports: Call for Evidence” about shore power (plugging ships into electricity so engines don't run) and other steps ports can take — we try to help remove barriers for ports to adopt cleaner tech.

turns.speaker: Martin Rhodes
turns.text: How do you measure aviation’s impact on local communities?

turns.speaker: Jennifer Raynor
turns.text: We publish economy-wide emissions stats. Local monitoring and air quality action plans pick up hotspots near airports; surface access (cars, buses to airports) is a big local part. We'll write with more detail on local aviation impacts.

turns.speaker: Jonathan Davies
turns.text: Electrification won't eliminate all problems. What are you doing to reduce traffic volumes in the most polluted areas?

turns.speaker: Simon Lightwood
turns.text: We're improving public transport and active travel so people have real choices. Measures include the £3 bus cap until end of 2026 (then £2 in 2027), free summer bus travel for children, rail fare freeze, major active-travel investment, and support via the Bus Services Act and local transport funding.

turns.speaker: Jonathan Davies
turns.text: Rural places struggle with services; many need cars. How do you help those who can’t afford EVs?

turns.speaker: Simon Lightwood
turns.text: The second-hand EV market is growing and getting cheaper — Autotrader showed EVs cheaper than petrol on average in April. We fund cross-pavement charging for people without off-street parking and commissioned a review of public charging prices (Philip New) to narrow the higher costs of public charging.

turns.speaker: John Whitby
turns.text: Any incentives for the second-hand EV market?

turns.speaker: Simon Lightwood
turns.text: Right now the market is driving prices down; no specific second-hand grant was proposed.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What’s the Government stance on London’s ULEZ (ultra low emission zone)? Should Government encourage mayors to take similar steps?

turns.speaker: Simon Lightwood
turns.text: Those decisions are for local leaders — we set national frameworks and provide funding. We are broadly agnostic, though we back local authorities with guidance and long-term transport funding and have provided £582 million specifically to support clean air zones where needed.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Local leaders need certainty of national support. Will you press Treasury to consider how taxes and incentives affect EV uptake and local decisions?

turns.speaker: Simon Lightwood
turns.text: Taxation is for HMT, but we’ll continue to press the case. We’ve committed £7.5 billion to 2035 for EVs (car grants, van/truck funds and charging). We’ve also consulted on a ZEV mandate and are not changing phase-out dates.

turns.speaker: Barry Gardiner
turns.text: Local mayors resist schemes when they lack certainty on support. Can you give them a national framework so they know what help they'll get if they act?

turns.speaker: Simon Lightwood
turns.text: I hear that and will write with more detail. We want devolved decision-making but with predictable funding so local leaders can act.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Final point: rather than just saying 'local decision', the Government should actively support mayors and explain the health benefits so the public demand action.

turns.speaker: Simon Lightwood
turns.text: We fund mayors and mayoral combined authorities, and there are examples, like bus franchising in Greater Manchester, which increased ridership. We will keep supporting local leaders to reduce emissions.

glossary.definition: The UK Department for Transport, the government department that makes and implements transport policy for roads, rail, buses and related services.
The UK Department for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs, responsible for environment, farming, food and rural policy.
A UK public agency that monitors and responds to public health threats and provides health protection advice.

glossary.term: Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government
glossary.definition: The UK government department (responsible for local government and housing finance) that manages local authority funding and community policy.
An expert advisory group that provides technical advice to government on air quality issues.
England's public body that enforces environmental protection, pollution control and regulation.
A government grant programme that helps farmers buy equipment and technology to reduce emissions and improve practices.
Farm methods and equipment for storing and handling animal manure (liquid waste) to reduce emissions like ammonia.
A forthcoming European vehicle emissions standard proposing stricter pollutant limits, including for brake and tyre wear particles.

glossary.term: Net Zero Ports: Call for Evidence
glossary.definition: A government consultation seeking input from ports and stakeholders on how ports can support net‑zero emissions goals.
A designated sea zone where ships must meet stricter legally enforced limits on pollutants such as sulphur and nitrogen oxides.
UK legislation that gives local authorities new powers to improve and organise bus services, including franchising options.
A system where a local authority specifies bus routes and standards and contracts operators to run them, instead of a deregulated market.
Groups of neighboring local councils led by a directly elected mayor that coordinate regional services like transport and planning.
HM Treasury, the UK government department responsible for public finance, economic policy and taxation.
A regulatory requirement for vehicle manufacturers to sell an increasing percentage of zero‑emission vehicles (electric or hydrogen) over time.
A formal public consultation where government requests information, data and views to inform future policy or legislation.
Local authority plans that identify pollution hotspots and set out measures to reduce air pollution in those areas.
